answers.java_tx_design: I haven't worked on a production Java backend -- my one year has been in Python, on Corvant's inventory module. I don't have a transaction-boundary story from Java specifically, so I'd rather not invent one.
answers.java_ops: Same answer as before: no Java, no JVM tuning. My operational experience is limited to a Django app -- I've watched a senior engineer tune our Gunicorn worker count after a memory spike, but I didn't do the tuning myself, just watched and took notes.
answers.rust_readiness: I haven't written Rust yet. My plan is to finish the official book this quarter, then rebuild a small internal script we have in Python -- a CSV-to-inventory-record importer -- in Rust, since it's self-contained and low-risk. I'd give myself three to four months before I'd trust my own Rust in anything real.
answers.rust_boundary: I don't have hands-on Rust experience to answer this from real practice. If I had to guess, I'd start with something stateless and easy to roll back, like a validation step, and keep the interface a plain HTTP call rather than anything more coupled. That's a guess, not something I've measured.
answers.money_correctness: I haven't built or operated an idempotency or reconciliation system myself. At Corvant we use idempotency keys on our order-import endpoint, but that was built before I joined, and I've only read the code, not designed or debugged it.
answers.incident_response: I haven't operated a system through an incident myself yet -- in my year at Corvant I've watched two, both handled by a senior engineer, and I mostly answered his questions about which inventory records looked affected. I haven't led one.
answers.process_skipping: Once, during a partial outage, I wanted to push a quick fix without waiting for review. I asked my lead first -- he said no, we'd rather be five minutes slower and sure -- so I waited, and review caught a bug in my fix. I haven't skipped one since.
answers.hiding_and_oncall: Two months in, I shipped a migration that silently dropped a default value. I told my manager the same day I noticed, before anyone else caught it. I'm on our support rotation one week a month, mostly triaging customer tickets, and I've mentored one newer intern on ticket triage.
answers.evidence_decision: I disagreed with a teammate over whether to cache a slow inventory query. I ran a load test showing the cache saved about 200ms per call, but the team decided against it anyway because of staleness risk. I accepted it and helped write the fallback instead.
answers.own_contribution: In the migration I described, the decision to keep the old default value wasn't mine -- my lead made that call. What was mine: I wrote the backfill script and picked the batch size, 500 rows at a time, after our first attempt at 5,000 timed out.
answers.java_recovery: No Java experience, so I don't have a Java recovery story. In Python, I once fixed a batch job that had stopped partway through an inventory reconciliation -- about 300 rows unprocessed -- by re-running it with a resume flag a senior engineer had added.
answers.java_perf_change: Same limitation -- no production Java. In Python, I added an index to a slow inventory-search query after profiling showed it as the top cost; response time went from around 900ms to 120ms. That's the only performance change I've made entirely on my own.
answers.rust_hands_on: I haven't written any Rust yet, production or personal -- not even a toy project. I've read through the ownership and borrowing chapters of the official book and done the exercises at the end of each, but I haven't opened an editor and started something real yet.
answers.rust_when_not: I don't have Rust experience, so I can't give a real example of holding back a rewrite in it. In general, I think anything stable and rarely touched shouldn't be rewritten just because a new language is exciting -- that's more instinct than something I've tested myself yet.
answers.reconciliation_mismatch: I haven't chased a numeric mismatch myself. I know the general causes -- time zones, rounding, late refunds -- from reading, but I don't have my own incident to describe, and I'd rather say that than make one up.
answers.prod_data_verification: I haven't been tempted to check something against production data -- at Corvant that's simply not allowed without a ticket and a DBA. When something doesn't reproduce in staging, I've asked a senior engineer to pull a masked copy rather than touch anything live myself.
